description: Daraa Mission Shield – درع حماية البعثات الفضائية: تطبيق تفاعلي يحاكي قاعدة فضائية على المريخ، يتعامل فيه المستخدم مع أزمات حقيقية مثل العواصف الترابية والإشعاع الشمسي ونقص الأكسجين والطاقة، ويرى أثر قراره على سلامة الطاقم واستمرار المهمة. نبني الأزمات على بيانات ناسا المفتوحة (DONKI وبيانات طقس المريخ وMOXIE) لتكون المحاكاة واقعية وتعليمية. نبحث عن مطور ويب، ومصمم واجهات، ومحلل بيانات. لا تشترط خبرة سابقة، يكفي الحماس والتعلم.
summary:
Daraa Mission Shield is an astronaut health monitoring and safety prototype we built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. It is a web dashboard that brings key health indicators into one clear view. Astronauts enter their indicators, and the platform compares them against configurable thresholds and their previous values. It then shows the results in charts and indicators, gives alerts and awareness guidance, and saves records so changes can be tracked over time.

It addresses the challenge by focusing on the hazards of long missions: changes in sleep and activity, different gravity, isolation and distance from Earth, and space radiation. We used NASA’s Human Research Program “Five Hazards of Human Spaceflight” to choose which risks and indicators matter most.

It matters because astronauts far from Earth need to understand their own condition quickly and early. The monitoring is rule-based, all data is simulated, and the interface supports Arabic and English.
details:
What it does and how it works

Daraa Mission Shield is a web dashboard that gathers an astronaut's key health indicators in one place. The user enters their indicators, such as sleep, activity and other readings. The platform compares each value against configurable thresholds and against the previous values. It then shows the results in clear charts and indicators, gives alerts and awareness guidance when something changes, and saves every record so the astronaut can follow their condition over time. The monitoring is purely rule-based, and all the data in the prototype is clearly labeled as simulated.

Benefits

  • Puts the important indicators in one clear view instead of scattered readings.
  • Helps astronauts notice changes early and understand them over time.
  • Gives simple awareness guidance when a value goes outside its threshold.
  • Keeps a saved history, so trends are easy to review.
  • Works in Arabic and English, with automatic RTL/LTR switching.

Intended impact

On long missions, astronauts are far from Earth and face changes in sleep and activity, different gravity, isolation, and space radiation. Daraa aims to help them follow their own condition and respond sooner. With technical integration and data accuracy checks, it could later receive data from sensors and approved health systems and be tested on more space scenarios.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Languages: HTML5, CSS3 and JavaScript only, with no external frameworks.
  • Charts and dashboards: built with JavaScript.
  • Software: Visual Studio Code, running locally with a simple local server.
  • Hardware: ordinary personal computers. No special hardware or sensors were used.
  • AI assistance: the platform itself contains no AI or machine learning. We used Claude by Anthropic to help write and refine the code, the presentation text and its English translation. All design decisions, content and testing were done by our team.

Creative side

We built the platform around NASA's Five Hazards of Human Spaceflight, so each section and indicator reflects a real spaceflight risk rather than a generic health tracker. The bilingual Arabic and English interface with full RTL/LTR switching is also uncommon in this kind of tool.

Factors we considered

  • Which health risks matter most, guided by NASA's Human Research Program.
  • Clarity and ease of use, so a non-expert can read the dashboard at a glance.
  • Honesty about the data: everything is simulated and labeled as such, and none of it is real NASA or astronaut data.
  • Transparency: the rule-based logic is easy to explain and check, with configurable thresholds.
  • Accessibility for Arabic and English speakers.
  • Future integration with real sensors and approved health systems, which would need data accuracy checks first.
